props.title: Demonlover
props.initialSlug: Corporate espionage turns deadly in cyber-porn war

sections.content: Demonlover represents Olivier Assayas's prescient dive into corporate espionage and digital exploitation. Like Videodrome (1983) before it, the film prophetically tackles how technology warps human consciousness and sexuality. Assayas crafts a labyrinthine thriller following Connie Nielsen's corporate executive Diane as she navigates a twisted world of anime porn rights, interactive torture websites, and ruthless business dealings. The film's cold, metallic aesthetics and Sonic Youth's droning score create an atmosphere of creeping digital dread that feels more relevant today than on release.

sections.content: The film exists in fascinating dialogue with other millennial tech-anxiety thrillers like eXistenZ (1999) and Pulse (2001). But where those films deal with virtual reality and internet haunting respectively, Demonlover focuses on the corporatization of digital depravity. The way it connects anime, pornography, and violence through multinational business deals feels especially prophetic of today's conversations around content moderation and digital ethics.

Assayas's clinical direction mirrors the sterile corporate environments while Connie Nielsen's purposefully opaque performance captures the moral emptiness at the story's center. The film shares DNA with Lost Highway (1997) in how it fragments narrative and identity, though Demonlover roots its surrealism in globalized capitalism rather than psychological horror. sections.content: While Demonlover lacks the explicit body horror of Cronenberg's works, it shares their fascination with how technology transforms human consciousness and sexuality. The film's infamous torture website "The Hellfire Club" predates discussions of the dark web while speaking to timeless anxieties about surveillance and consent. Like Strange Days (1995), it recognizes how new media technologies create novel forms of exploitation.
